subject: chemistry
question_text: Write the general properties of ionic compounds.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book lists six properties; the card groups them into four marked lines (state with melting points, solubility, conductivity, reactivity with isomerism), each carrying its reason.

steps.label: State, melting and boiling points
lines: 2. Melting and boiling points are high,
the ions in the crystal lattice.
steps.why: Both properties come from the same cause: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds them in fixed positions in a rigid lattice that needs much energy to break.
common_mistakes: Stating high melting point without the reason. The electrostatic-forces sentence is part of the mark.
steps.memory_tip: Strong forces between ions: solid crystals, high melting point — one cause, two properties.
steps.margin_note: Attach the reason to the property in the same sentence.

steps.label: Solubility
lines: in polar solvents such as water and liquid
steps.why: Polar solvent molecules attract the ions and separate them from the lattice; non-polar solvents cannot attract charged particles, so the lattice stays intact.
common_mistakes: Writing soluble in all solvents. The polar or non-polar distinction IS the property.
Giving no example solvent. Water is expected.
steps.memory_tip: Charged ions dissolve in polar solvents; polar dissolves polar.
steps.margin_note: Name one polar and one non-polar solvent.

steps.label: Electrical conductivity
lines: in the solid state, because the ions are
Good conductors in the molten state and in
aqueous solution, because the ions are
steps.why: Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. The same ions are present in both states; only their freedom to move changes, which is why the property flips.
common_mistakes: Writing that ionic solids conduct. In the solid the ions cannot move, so it does not conduct.
Saying electrons carry the current. In molten and dissolved ionic compounds the IONS carry it.
steps.memory_tip: Fixed ions, no current. Free ions (molten or dissolved), current flows.
steps.margin_note: The property is in two halves — solid against molten or dissolved. Write both.

steps.label: Reactivity and isomerism
lines: aqueous solution are very fast, because

lines.text: Fast reactions in solution; no isomerism

lines: 6. The ionic bond is non-directional, so
ionic compounds do not show isomerism.
steps.why: The last two book properties share one theme: what the ionic bond is (a non-directional attraction between free ions) fixes both the reaction speed and the absence of isomerism.
common_mistakes: Writing that ionic compounds show isomerism. The bond has no fixed direction, so there are no distinct arrangements.
Giving the isomerism fact without its non-directional reason.
steps.memory_tip: No direction to the bond, so no different arrangements — no isomerism.
steps.margin_note: Six properties in total across the four lines matches the book's list.

insider_note: Attach the reason to each property — high melting point BECAUSE of strong electrostatic forces. A property without its reason is half the mark.
